blocks.text:
Design the core money-movement engine behind a digital wallet platform (the kind that powers peer-to-peer transfers, top-ups, and withdrawals). Two guarantees make this problem genuinely different from a typical CRUD service: every transaction must be recorded as a balanced double-entry ledger, exactly the way real accounting systems work, and every transaction must be safe to retry, since a client's network request can time out even after the server successfully processed it, and retrying must never double-charge anyone.

  • Actors: User (sends transfers, tops up, withdraws), WalletService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: peer-to-peer transfers, top-ups, withdrawals with fees, a double-entry ledger, and idempotency-key-based deduplication.

The distinguishing mechanic is exactly-once money movement: every transaction is deduplicated by an idempotency key before any balance changes, and every successful transaction writes a balanced set of debit and credit ledger entries, an accounting invariant no prior design in this series has needed.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Transfer funds: move money from one wallet to another, identified by an idempotency key supplied by the caller.
Top up a wallet: add funds from an external source into a wallet.
Withdraw funds: move money out of a wallet to an external bank account, subject to a withdrawal fee.
Deduplicate retries: if the same idempotency key is submitted again, return the original transaction's result without reprocessing it.
Maintain a ledger: every successful transaction writes one or more balanced debit and credit entries that can reconstruct any wallet's balance.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting millions of wallets and transactions must not require touching existing transfer logic.
Extensibility: a new fee model or transaction type should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: fee rules, notification, and id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: checking whether an idempotency key was already seen, and applying a balance update, are both constant-time lookups.
Thread safety: two transfers touching the same wallet concurrently must never both read the same stale balance.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: How long should an idempotency key remain valid before it can be reused for a different request?
Should transfers support multiple currencies, or is a single currency assumed?
Is overdraft or a negative balance ever allowed, for any wallet?
Should the ledger be the source of truth for balance, computed by summing entries, or is a cached running balance acceptable for fast reads?
Should fees vary per user tier, or is a single fee model applied uniformly?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: A single currency is assumed throughout; multi-currency conversion is out of scope.
An idempotency key never expires in this design, it is checked for the lifetime of the system, noted as a simplification versus a real TTL-bounded key store.
A wallet's balance is maintained as a running total for fast reads, while the ledger independently records every movement for audit and integrity verification.
No wallet may go negative; every transaction is validated against the current balance before it is applied.
Peer-to-peer transfers are free; only withdrawals to an external bank incur a fee.

blocks.text: The design centers on four core entities:

metadata.alt: Core entities: Wallet, Transaction, LedgerEntry, and IdempotencyRecord

items: Wallet: an owner's running balance.
Transaction: one transfer, top-up, or withdrawal request, keyed by its idempotency key.
LedgerEntry: one debit or credit line item produced by a transaction.
IdempotencyRecord: maps a previously-seen idempotency key back to its resulting transaction.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A wallet participates in many transactions as sender or receiver; every transaction produces two or more always-balanced ledger entries; every transaction is keyed by its idempotency record

items: Wallet to Transaction is one-to-many, in either the sender or receiver role.
Transaction to LedgerEntry always produces a balanced set: total debits equal total credits.
Transaction to IdempotencyRecord is a one-to-one keying relationship.

blocks.text: Three patterns keep fee rules, notification, and id creation decoupled from the core service.

Why needed: a peer-to-peer transfer and a withdrawal to an external bank charge fundamentally different fees, free versus a percentage of the amount, and that is exactly the kind of decision that varies by transaction type.

metadata.alt: FeeStrategy interface with NoFeeStrategy and PercentageFeeStrategy implementations

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a new fee model (a flat fee, a tiered fee by user level) is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to the core transfer logic in WalletService. What it solves: it isolates fee-calculation rules from the shared, stable ledger-writing algorithm.
Why needed: a transaction succeeding, being rejected, or being detected as a duplicate are all events a real wallet platform would want to react to (push notifications, fraud monitoring, analytics).

metadata.alt: WalletObserver interface notified by WalletService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: WalletService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core transaction workflow from side effects.
Why needed: transaction and ledger entry id generation should not be scattered across calling code.

metadata.alt: TransactionIdFactory generating sequential TXN and LE prefixed ids

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: every transaction and ledger entry is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Wallet: attributes walletId, ownerName, balance; responsibility: track one owner's current spendable balance.
Transaction: attributes transactionId, idempotencyKey, fromWalletId, toWalletId, amount, fee, type, status; responsibility: represent one completed or rejected money movement.
LedgerEntry: attributes entryId, walletId, transactionId, entryType, amount; responsibility: record one balanced debit or credit line.
WalletService: the orchestrator; responsibility: deduplicate by idempotency key, validate balances, write the ledger, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: FeeStrategy and WalletObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: FeeStrategy: calculateFee(amount): abstracts away exactly how much a transaction type costs to process.
WalletObserver: onTransactionProcessed / onTransactionRejected / onDuplicateDetected: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover a successful transfer, a deduplicated retry of that same transfer, and a withdrawal with a percentage fee.

metadata.alt: Alice transfers 200 to Bob; the idempotency key is new, so the transfer is validated, ledgered, and applied
Alice retries the same request with the same idempotency key after a timeout; the service returns the original result without reprocessing
Bob withdraws 100; a 2 percent fee is calculated, and the ledger splits the debit into an external-bank credit and a fee-collection credit

blocks.text: The deduplicate-then-transfer workflow, alongside its rejection branches, looks like this:

metadata.alt: Check the idempotency key first, then validate balance, then write balanced ledger entries and update both wallets

items: Happy path, new key: submit with a fresh idempotency key → balance covers amount plus fee → debit sender, credit receiver, write ledger entries → record the key → return the new transaction.
Happy path, duplicate key: submit with a previously-seen idempotency key → return the exact same transaction from before, with zero balance changes.

Rejection path: submit with a fresh idempotency key → balance does not cover amount plus fee → rejected, and this outcome is not remembered against the key, so a corrected retry with the same key can still succeed.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: transfer(fromWalletId, toWalletId, amount, idempotencyKey): moves funds between two wallets, free of fees.
withdraw(walletId, amount, idempotencyKey): moves funds to an external bank, applying the configured fee strategy.
verifyLedgerIntegrity(): confirms the system-wide invariant that total debits equal total credits across every ledger entry ever written.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: InsufficientBalanceException: a wallet cannot cover the requested amount plus any applicable fee.
WalletNotFoundException: an unknown wallet id was referenced.
InvalidTransactionException: a self-transfer or a non-positive amount was requested.

blocks.text: The critical race is two transfers touching the same wallet at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to debit the same wallet; synchronization ensures one transaction commits fully before the other reads the balance

blocks.text: Synchronizing the validate-and-apply step per wallet ensures a balance is never read stale by a second transfer, which would otherwise let both transfers succeed against a balance that could only actually cover one of them.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new fee model (a flat withdrawal fee, a tiered fee by account level) is a new FeeStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (push notification, fraud alert) is a new WalletObserver implementation.
Multi-currency support can be layered on by adding a currency field and a conversion step ahead of the existing balance checks.
A time-bounded idempotency key expiry can be added by attaching a timestamp to each IdempotencyRecord and checking it before treating a key as still valid.
Single Responsibility: Wallet tracks balance, FeeStrategy decides fee rules, WalletObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new fee models or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to WalletService.
Liskov Substitution: any FeeStrategy or WalletObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: WalletObserver exposes only the three lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: WalletService depends on the FeeStrategy and WalletObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.

A retried request with the same idempotency key but a DIFFERENT amount or receiver is still treated as a duplicate and returns the original result, since the key alone identifies the request, an explicit assumption worth calling out.
A rejected transaction is never recorded against its idempotency key, so a client can safely correct the request (for example, after topping up) and retry with the same key.
A withdrawal whose fee alone would push the total above the balance is rejected exactly like an insufficient-balance transfer, since fee is included in the affordability check.
verifyLedgerIntegrity must hold after every single transaction, not just at the end, since a bug that unbalances even one transaction should be caught immediately in testing.
transfer / withdraw: O(1) for the idempotency lookup, balance check, and balance update; O(k) to write k ledger entries, where k is small and fixed per transaction type.
verifyLedgerIntegrity: O(n) where n is the total number of ledger entries ever written.
Space: O(wallets + transactions + ledger entries) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Wallet, Transaction, LedgerEntry, and IdempotencyRecord

items: A unique index on Transaction(idempotencyKey) makes the deduplication check itself an atomic, race-free database operation.
LedgerEntry is append-only, rows are never updated or deleted, which is what makes it trustworthy for reconstructing balance history.
Add a time-bounded expiry to idempotency keys instead of retaining them forever.
Support multi-currency wallets with a conversion step.
Add tiered fee models based on account level or transaction volume.
In a distributed deployment, shard wallets across multiple database nodes and use a distributed transaction or saga pattern for cross-shard transfers.

blocks.text: TransactionType, TransactionStatus, EntryType, Wallet, LedgerEntry, Transaction, and TransactionIdFactory:

codes.python:
from enum import Enum

# The kind of movement a transaction represents.
class TransactionType(Enum):
    TRANSFER = "TRANSFER"
    TOPUP = "TOPUP"
    WITHDRAWAL = "WITHDRAWAL"

# The outcome of a transaction attempt.
class TransactionStatus(Enum):
    SUCCESS = "SUCCESS"
    REJECTED = "REJECTED"

# Which side of a balanced ledger line this entry represents.
class EntryType(Enum):
    DEBIT = "DEBIT"
    CREDIT = "CREDIT"

# A single owner's spendable balance.
class Wallet:
    def __init__(self, wallet_id, owner_name, balance):
        self.wallet_id = wallet_id      # unique id
        self.owner_name = owner_name      # display name
        self.balance = balance              # current spendable balance

    def adjust_balance(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount  # add or subtract balance

# One balanced debit or credit line produced by a transaction.
class LedgerEntry:
    def __init__(self, entry_id, wallet_id, transaction_id, entry_type, amount):
        self.entry_id = entry_id            # unique id, e.g. LE1
        self.wallet_id = wallet_id            # which wallet this line affects
        self.transaction_id = transaction_id    # which transaction produced this line
        self.entry_type = entry_type              # debit or credit
        self.amount = amount                        # amount of this line

# One transfer, top-up, or withdrawal request.
class Transaction:
    def __init__(self, transaction_id, idempotency_key, from_wallet_id, to_wallet_id, amount, fee, tx_type, status):
        self.transaction_id = transaction_id      # unique id, e.g. TXN1
        self.idempotency_key = idempotency_key      # caller-supplied dedup key
        self.from_wallet_id = from_wallet_id          # sender, None for a top-up
        self.to_wallet_id = to_wallet_id                 # receiver, None for a withdrawal
        self.amount = amount                               # requested amount
        self.fee = fee                                       # fee charged, if any
        self.type = tx_type                                    # transfer, top-up, or withdrawal
        self.status = status                                     # success or rejected

# Creates sequential, correctly-prefixed ids for transactions and ledger entries.
class TransactionIdFactory:
    def __init__(self):
        self.transaction_counter = 0  # running id counter for transactions
        self.entry_counter = 0          # running id counter for ledger entries

    def next_transaction_id(self):
        self.transaction_counter += 1  # bump id counter
        return f"TXN{self.transaction_counter}"  # e.g. TXN1

    def next_ledger_entry_id(self):
        self.entry_counter += 1  # bump id counter
        return f"LE{self.entry_counter}"  # e.g. LE1

WalletService, including the transfer, withdraw and ledger integrity logic:

codes.python:
# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class InsufficientBalanceException(Exception): pass
class WalletNotFoundException(Exception): pass
class InvalidTransactionException(Exception): pass

# The core money-movement engine tying every piece together.
class WalletService:
    EXTERNAL_BANK = "EXTERNAL_BANK"    # pseudo wallet for outbound funds
    FEE_COLLECTION = "FEE_COLLECTION"    # pseudo wallet for collected fees

    def __init__(self):
        self.wallets = {}            # walletId -> Wallet
        self.idempotency_store = {}    # idempotencyKey -> Transaction
        self.ledger = []                 # every ledger line ever written
        self.observers = []                 # listeners
        self.wallets[self.EXTERNAL_BANK] = Wallet(self.EXTERNAL_BANK, "External Bank", 0.0)     # register the external sink
        self.wallets[self.FEE_COLLECTION] = Wallet(self.FEE_COLLECTION, "Fee Collection", 0.0)  # register the fee sink

    def add_wallet(self, wallet):
        self.wallets[wallet.wallet_id] = wallet  # register a real wallet

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def _write_entry(self, wallet_id, transaction_id, entry_type, amount, factory):
        self.ledger.append(LedgerEntry(factory.next_ledger_entry_id(), wallet_id, transaction_id, entry_type, amount))  # append one ledger line

    def transfer(self, from_wallet_id, to_wallet_id, amount, idempotency_key, factory):
        if idempotency_key in self.idempotency_store:  # already processed this exact request
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_duplicate_detected(idempotency_key)  # notify
            return self.idempotency_store[idempotency_key]  # return the original result untouched
        if from_wallet_id == to_wallet_id:
            raise InvalidTransactionException("Cannot transfer to the same wallet")  # reject self-transfer
        if amount <= 0:
            raise InvalidTransactionException("Amount must be positive")  # reject non-positive amount
        from_wallet = self.wallets.get(from_wallet_id)  # sender
        to_wallet = self.wallets.get(to_wallet_id)         # receiver
        if from_wallet is None or to_wallet is None:
            raise WalletNotFoundException("Unknown wallet")  # reject unknown wallet
        fee_strategy = NoFeeStrategy()  # peer-to-peer transfers are free
        fee = fee_strategy.calculate_fee(amount)  # compute fee, zero here
        if from_wallet.balance < amount + fee:  # not enough funds
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_transaction_rejected(from_wallet_id, "Insufficient balance")  # notify
            raise InsufficientBalanceException(f"Not enough balance in {from_wallet_id}")
        transaction_id = factory.next_transaction_id()  # build id
        from_wallet.adjust_balance(-amount)  # debit sender
        to_wallet.adjust_balance(amount)  # credit receiver
        self._write_entry(from_wallet_id, transaction_id, EntryType.DEBIT, amount, factory)  # ledger debit line
        self._write_entry(to_wallet_id, transaction_id, EntryType.CREDIT, amount, factory)  # ledger credit line
        transaction = Transaction(transaction_id, idempotency_key, from_wallet_id, to_wallet_id, amount, fee, TransactionType.TRANSFER, TransactionStatus.SUCCESS)
        self.idempotency_store[idempotency_key] = transaction  # remember this key's result
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_transaction_processed(transaction)  # notify
        return transaction  # hand back the completed transaction

    def withdraw(self, wallet_id, amount, idempotency_key, factory):
        if idempotency_key in self.idempotency_store:  # already processed this exact request
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_duplicate_detected(idempotency_key)  # notify
            return self.idempotency_store[idempotency_key]  # return the original result untouched
        if amount <= 0:
            raise InvalidTransactionException("Amount must be positive")  # reject non-positive amount
        wallet = self.wallets.get(wallet_id)  # withdrawing wallet
        if wallet is None:
            raise WalletNotFoundException("Unknown wallet")  # reject unknown wallet
        fee_strategy = PercentageFeeStrategy(0.02)  # withdrawals charge 2 percent
        fee = fee_strategy.calculate_fee(amount)  # compute fee
        if wallet.balance < amount + fee:  # not enough funds
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_transaction_rejected(wallet_id, "Insufficient balance")  # notify
            raise InsufficientBalanceException(f"Not enough balance in {wallet_id}")
        transaction_id = factory.next_transaction_id()  # build id
        wallet.adjust_balance(-(amount + fee))  # debit the full amount plus fee
        self.wallets[self.EXTERNAL_BANK].adjust_balance(amount)  # funds leave to the external bank
        self.wallets[self.FEE_COLLECTION].adjust_balance(fee)  # fee collected internally
        self._write_entry(wallet_id, transaction_id, EntryType.DEBIT, amount + fee, factory)  # ledger debit line
        self._write_entry(self.EXTERNAL_BANK, transaction_id, EntryType.CREDIT, amount, factory)  # ledger credit to external bank
        self._write_entry(self.FEE_COLLECTION, transaction_id, EntryType.CREDIT, fee, factory)  # ledger credit to fee collection
        transaction = Transaction(transaction_id, idempotency_key, wallet_id, self.EXTERNAL_BANK, amount, fee, TransactionType.WITHDRAWAL, TransactionStatus.SUCCESS)
        self.idempotency_store[idempotency_key] = transaction  # remember this key's result
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_transaction_processed(transaction)  # notify
        return transaction  # hand back the completed transaction

    def verify_ledger_integrity(self):
        total_debits = 0.0    # running debit total
        total_credits = 0.0     # running credit total
        for entry in self.ledger:  # scan every ledger line ever written
            if entry.entry_type == EntryType.DEBIT:
                total_debits += entry.amount  # accumulate debits
            else:
                total_credits += entry.amount  # accumulate credits
        return abs(total_debits-total_credits) < 0.0001  # true only if the books balance

    def get_wallet(self, wallet_id):
        return self.wallets.get(wallet_id)  # wallet lookup, used by the demo to print balances

items: Why check the idempotency key before validating balance, rather than after? Because the entire point of the key is to make retries a complete no-op, and running balance checks against a request that has already succeeded once would risk observably different behavior (or worse, a race) on the retry.

Why model a withdrawal as touching three wallets (the real one, an external bank sink, and a fee collection sink) instead of just debiting one balance? Because it keeps the accounting invariant strictly true for every transaction type, not just transfers, which is exactly what makes verifyLedgerIntegrity meaningful as a system-wide sanity check rather than a special case.

How would you extend this to support a real, time-bounded idempotency window? Store a timestamp on each IdempotencyRecord and check it is still within the allowed window before treating a key as a valid duplicate, otherwise treat it as a brand new request.

Cached running balance vs balance-by-ledger-replay: a cached balance on Wallet gives O(1) reads, at the cost of needing careful synchronization to keep it consistent with the ledger; recomputing balance by summing ledger entries on every read would be always-correct by construction but far slower at scale.

Idempotency keys never expiring vs a time-bounded window: never expiring is simpler to reason about and impossible to get wrong by reusing a key too early, at the cost of an ever-growing store; a real system would need an expiry policy to bound memory.

Synchronous ledger writes vs asynchronous, eventually-consistent ledger writes: synchronous writes (used here) guarantee the ledger and the balance are never out of sync, at the cost of coupling transaction latency to ledger write latency; an async approach would need a reconciliation process to catch drift.

Persist wallets, transactions, ledger entries, and idempotency records in a relational database with the unique constraint on idempotencyKey enforced at the database level, not just in application code.
Emit transaction events to a message queue so downstream systems (notifications, fraud detection, analytics) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Run a periodic reconciliation job that recomputes every wallet balance from the ledger and alerts on any drift from the cached balance.
Rate-limit and monitor withdrawal requests per wallet to catch abuse patterns that a single-transaction validation cannot see.
